title: Holes
full_review:
A pair of stolen sneakers which have fallen from the sky puts a teen-age boy in reform camp where his century-old family curse finally comes full circle in "Holes" (Disney).

Unlucky Stanley Yelnats (played by Shia LaBeouf, his last name is his first name spelled backward, or is it the other way around?) is sentenced to 18 months in a camp for troubled youth when he is assumed to have stolen a basketball star's prized sneaks.

The reform camp is in the middle of the desert, 100 miles from the nearest water, so no need for guards and fences. Owned by the seldom-seen warden (Sigourney Weaver), the cruel overseer (Jon Voight in villainous moustache and pompadour do) makes the boys dig deep holes all day, every day, without explanation. And the downtrodden youngsters are none too welcoming to Stanley, whose disastrous family history is played out in flashbacks that are livelier than the contemporary story.

It seems Stanley's ancestor in the old country inadvertently crossed a Gypsy fortune teller (Eartha Kitt) who put a multigenerational curse on him as he headed off to seek his fortune in America's Old West. Sure enough, misfortune came his way when outlaw Kissin' Kate Barlow (Patricia Arquette) crossed his path and relieved him of his treasure chest. We also learn Kate was once a sweet schoolmarm whose affection for a kindly black man (Dule Hill) had dire consequences leading to her change of career.

Meanwhile, the hole-digging intensifies as Stanley befriends pint-size Zero (Khleo Thomas), who risks death by running off, eventually followed by Stanley, and together they unravel the mystery of the holes and their shared ancestral past.

Director Andrew Davis has a great deal of story to tell, based on the popular juvenile novel of the same name by Louis Sachar. It may be more exciting to read than to see, though, as the film loses energy whenever it returns from the Old West segments to the hole diggers. But humorous scenes return to Stanley's struggling family, where his inventor dad (Henry Winkler) is determined to find the formula for smell-less shoes.

Nonetheless, several characters are one-dimensional. Voight hams it up a bit much, but Weaver is comically effective as the steely proprietress of the camp -- so tough she paints her fingernails with snake venom. LaBeouf and Thomas are appealing in their roles but the movie is an odd mixture of nice with nasty, considering it's aimed at children. The feel-good ending is a crowd-pleaser that so ties up every story strand it's hard to overlook the movie's far-fetched coincidences.

But with its themes of friendship and family values, coupled with pleasing visuals, older children may just dig "Holes."

Because of brief violence and a crass expression, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
